characters: Madam Yartey: the agricultural science teacher, in a bright dress, holding a set of role cards.
Sumaiya Aidoo: a 13-year-old girl playing the farmer, holding a bunch of cassava.
Wumpini Amankwa: a 14-year-old boy playing the processor, with a bowl of gari.
The class: twelve pupils standing in a line with role cards hung round their necks.

narrationPlan.voice: A lively, organised voice for Madam Yartey; bright, varied voices for the pupils
narrationPlan.pace: Brisk and playful in the game, slower for the Rwanda page and the summary (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quick, playful drum and flute for the game; a calm, steady tune for the summary (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Madam Yartey, Sumaiya, Wumpini and the class are invented. The prices in the cassava example are imaginary and labelled so. The statement that selling at harvest was linked to a loss of about 29 per cent of grain sales value comes from a study cited in a 2018 IFPRI paper on post-harvest loss.

The Rwanda facts come from a trade article that is not recent: aid-funded projects built washing stations and organised cooperatives from 2000; specialty coffee is fully washed, scores above 85 points and is traceable; about 27 per cent of exported coffee is specialty, up from almost none in 2000; it sells for 15 to 25 per cent above market prices; one cooperative manager says his income is about five times what it was before 2001. The manager’s figure is his own account, and the story says so.
The story does not say middlemen are villains: it shows that each link has costs and risks, and it asks the class to find the one small step a crop in their own district needs.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have an agribusiness specialist check the cassava chain description and the idea of value addition, and replace the imaginary prices with real local ones in class.
Check the Rwanda figures against a more recent source, and check the date of the trade article, then update or label the figures as dated.
Check the summary-writing tip and the word count (43 words) against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story that turns a classroom into a farm-to-table chain, with a Rwandan example of cooperatives and shared processing. It models a summary of 45 words or fewer.
learningGoals: Name six links in a farm-to-market chain and say one cost or risk for each.
Explain value addition with an example.
Write a summary of 45 words or fewer that keeps the main points.
beforeReading: Ask: who has handled the food on your plate before it reached you?
whileReading: At page 2, let learners act the chain with real or paper props.
afterReading: Draw the chain for a food your family eats and mark one place where it could be improved.
Write a 45-word summary of the lesson.
discussion: Why might the farmer and the shopkeeper see the prices differently?
What did the Rwandan example need besides cooperatives?
reflection: If you were a link in a food chain, which would you choose and why?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose cassava sells at GH¢100 and the gari made from it sells at GH¢250. What is the difference, and what percentage of the selling price is it?
A summary must be 45 words or fewer. A pupil writes 43 words. How many words are left?

support: Give a summary frame: one sentence on the chain, one on value addition, one on the Rwanda example, one on what Ghana could do.
stretch: Write a report recommending one small step for a crop in your district, with a heading, an introduction, findings and a recommendation.

The Rwanda facts come from a trade article that is not recent: aid-funded projects built washing stations and organised cooperatives from 2000; specialty coffee is fully washed, scores above 85 points and is traceable; about 27 per cent of exported coffee is specialty, up from almost none in 2000; it sells for 15 to 25 per cent above market prices; one cooperative manager says his income is about five times what it was before 2001. localiseThis: Visit or interview a local processor (with an adult) such as a gari or oil processor and use real costs and prices.

factCheck.claim: Rwanda’s specialty coffee grew from almost none in 2000 to about 27 per cent of coffee exports after aid-funded projects built washing stations and organised farmers into cooperatives; it sells for 15 to 25 per cent above market prices; one cooperative manager says his income is about five times what it was before 2001.
factCheck.explanation: From a trade article that is not recent; the manager’s figure is his own account.
factCheck.reference: How we made it in Africa, “How Rwanda is making a name for itself in ‘specialty’ coffee” (howwemadeitinafrica.com).

factCheck.claim: One study cited in a 2018 paper linked selling grain straight after harvest to a loss equal to 29.3 per cent of grain sales value because of seasonal price swings.
factCheck.explanation: A figure from a study cited in the paper, not from the paper’s own data.
factCheck.reference: Baral, S. and Hoffmann, V. (2018), IFPRI Working Paper on post-harvest loss in Ghana (cgspace.cgiar.org).
